## WPC513 — Westside Property Care
### Business Operations Manual — 4-Client Model

This is the model I would lock in for the first phase of WPC. The objective is not volume.
It is four good residential clients, predictable recurring revenue, excellent service, and
enough open capacity to handle profitable project work without WPC taking over your week.

### 1. Core business model

- Recurring-client cap: 4 properties
- Membership: $229/month per property
- Frequency: 2 scheduled visits per month
- Recurring visits: 8/month
- Routine service days: Monday and Friday
- Tuesday–Thursday: project work, customer-requested work, emergencies and estimates
- Weekend: no regularly scheduled WPC work

Financial baseline:

| Metric | Target |
|---|---|
| Recurring clients | 4 |
| Revenue/client | $229/month |
| Recurring revenue | $916/month |
| Recurring revenue | $10,992/year |
| Visits | 8/month |
| Visits | 96/year |
| Target average visit | ~80 minutes |
| Routine field labor | ~10.7 hrs/month |
| Routine field labor | ~128 hrs/year |

The 80-minute target is internal. It does not need to appear in customer-facing materials.
You're selling ongoing property care, not minutes.

### 2. What the customer is buying

**WPC Residential Property Care Membership — $229/month, 2 scheduled visits monthly**

The purpose is simple: keep the home's outdoor living areas clean, maintained and ready to
enjoy while identifying small problems before they become larger ones.

A routine visit may include, as applicable to the property:

- Quick exterior property inspection
- Pool skimming
- Pool skimmer/pump basket emptying
- Light leaf, stick and debris pickup
- Outdoor trash emptied into homeowner's designated cans
- Patio and outdoor furniture wipe-down
- Outdoor countertops wiped down
- Stainless-steel surfaces wiped down
- Flat-top/grill grease trap emptied
- Hard surfaces blown clean
- Flower pots watered
- Very light weed treatment when appropriate
- General outdoor-living-area organization
- Identification of items needing additional attention

Important: Not every task has to be performed every visit. Work is prioritized according to
what the property needs.

### 3. What is NOT included

This is where you protect the $229 model.

Routine membership does not include: deep grill cleaning, pressure washing, major storm
cleanup, landscaping projects, drainage installation, repairs, replacement parts,
large-volume debris removal, extensive weeding, gutter cleaning, window-well cleanouts,
heavy hauling or anything requiring specialized materials/equipment.

Those become separately quoted projects. Materials and replacement parts should also be
billed separately.

Your recurring service should find additional work, not absorb additional work.

### 4. Monthly operating schedule

With four clients, I wouldn't spread eight visits over every Monday and Friday.
Consolidate them.

- **Week 1** — Monday: Client A, Client B. Friday: Client C, Client D.
- **Week 2** — No mandatory recurring visits. Use Monday/Friday for weather rescheduling,
  projects, estimates or leave them open.
- **Week 3** — Monday: Client A, Client B. Friday: Client C, Client D.
- **Week 4** — Again, no mandatory recurring visits.

That is an extremely comfortable schedule. You effectively have four core recurring workdays
per month. Even if you spend 2–3 hours including driving on each route, you're looking at
roughly 8–12 total route hours per month depending on geography.

### 5. Route strategy

Client selection matters almost as much as pricing. Ideally:

- Clients A & B: geographically close
- Clients C & D: geographically close

Don't accept a $229 customer who requires 40 minutes of driving each way unless there's a
strategic reason. The four-property model becomes much more profitable when the route is
compact.

Eventually you want to be able to say: Monday route: 2 nearby homes. Friday route: 2 nearby homes.

### 6. Standard operating procedure — every visit

**Before arrival:** Review the previous service report and any homeowner requests. Check
weather. Load required routine supplies.

**Upon arrival:** Do a quick walk around before starting. Look for storm damage, standing
water, fallen limbs, pool issues, excessive debris, outdoor kitchen problems, drainage
issues, furniture damage, anything visibly unusual. Take a picture when something deserves
documentation.

**Perform routine service:** Work through the property's priorities. The goal isn't "How
many things can I check off?" It's "What will make the biggest difference to this property
today?"

**Before leaving:** Do another walkthrough. Check gates. Make sure equipment and supplies are
removed. Take after-service pictures where useful. Send/update the service record.

### 7. Customer communication system

This is one of the areas where a four-client operation can outperform larger companies.
After each visit, send something simple:

**WPC SERVICE COMPLETE ✓**

Then briefly tell them what was handled. Example:

> Today's property care is complete. Pool skimmed and baskets emptied, patio and furniture
> cleaned, outdoor kitchen surfaces wiped down, loose debris collected, flower pots watered
> and hard surfaces blown clean.
>
> I also noticed debris accumulating in the window wells. I recommend cleaning those during
> an upcoming visit. I can add that for $49.

That communication makes the $229 membership tangible. The homeowner knows you were there,
what you did, and what you're watching.

### 8. Property record

Maintain a simple file for each of the four homes.

```
CLIENT A
Customer:              Water access:
Address:               Electrical access:
Phone:                 Special instructions:
Gate/access:           Pets:
Preferred communication:  Known property issues:
Service days:          Recommended future projects:
Pool information:
Grill/outdoor kitchen:
Trash location:
```

Then maintain a service history:

| Date | Visit | Work Completed | Issues Found | Add-On |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8/3 | #1 | Routine care | Window wells | $49 |
| 8/17 | #2 | Routine care | None | — |

With only four properties, this can become extremely detailed.

### 9. Add-on/project model

This is where WPC can make substantially more money without needing more recurring customers.

- Grill/outdoor kitchen deep cleaning: $249+
- Window-well cleaning: $49+
- Pressure washing: quoted
- Storm cleanup: quoted
- Drainage correction: quoted
- Outdoor repairs: quoted
- Seasonal cleanup: quoted
- Special property projects: quoted

Consider one simple example. Four memberships produce $10,992/year. If each household
purchases just two $249 projects per year: 8 × $249 = $1,992. Total: $12,984/year. And
that's still only four recurring customers.

### 10. One-time customer strategy

You can still accept non-members. I'd use Tuesday–Thursday primarily for these jobs. If
someone wants a $249 grill cleaning, do the grill cleaning. But that customer also becomes a
potential membership lead.

You don't need 50 recurring customers. You need four excellent ones. Once all four
membership positions are filled, the website can legitimately say **CURRENT MEMBERSHIP:
FULL** or **Join the WPC Property Care Waitlist**. That's considerably more premium than
constantly trying to fill a route.

### 11. Financial operating rules

Track three numbers separately:

- **Recurring revenue** — $916/month. This is your predictable base.
- **Project revenue** — anything outside membership.
- **Materials** — materials should not disappear into labor revenue. If a project requires
  $75 worth of materials, track the $75 separately so you can see your actual margin.

At the end of every month, your WPC report should show: membership revenue, project revenue,
material reimbursements, total gross revenue, materials/expenses, net operating profit, hours
worked, effective hourly rate. That last number matters.

### 12. Capacity rule

Four memberships is the target AND the cap. Don't get four customers and immediately think
"I could probably squeeze in another six."

The excess capacity is part of the product. It gives you room for weather delays, a property
needing extra attention, vacations, family obligations, equipment issues, estimates,
profitable projects, emergency customer requests, and simply having time off.

You're deliberately giving up maximum revenue in exchange for control and service quality.

### 13. Membership standard

I'd establish five internal rules:

1. Never rush a property because another client is waiting.
2. Communicate anything unusual.
3. Leave the property visibly better than you found it.
